newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish June inflation seen stable, market unfazed.
newsitem.headline: Irish June inflation seen stable, market unfazed.

text.p: Irish inflation data this week should show consumer price pressure remained moderate in June despite currency weakness, with the bond market seen taking the numbers in stride, analysts said on Monday.
Analysts predicted June consumer price index figures on Thursday would show a monthly rise of 0.2 percent, the same as May's level.
Year-on-year data was not available due to a lack of data for last June, analysts said.
"We don't think the generalised inflation problem is huge as of yet. The currency effects are only feeding through to a very minimal extent at this stage," said NCB stockbrokers economist Eunan King.
As a result, the bond and currency markets were expected to shrug off the data.
"The market has a concern about rising inflation that's in some sense priced in there. So I don't think 0.2 percent is going to affect it one way or the other," King said.
"You're going to need 0.3 percent or above to cause the markets to take any great notice of it," he added.
Analysts did not expect the Irish pound's recent sharp fall to translate into broadly higher prices until later this year, mainly because companies had already hedged their currency exposure.

"A lot of them have probably covered forward their needs, so that kind of takes the next three to six months out of their perspective. They don't have to change prices very quickly because they're not actually being affected by today's spot rate," King said.
AIB Group Treasury's bond unit said their own supermarket survey found that prices on some exchange-rate sensitive goods had crept up over the past couple of months.
"But these rises are not excessive and are still not across the board," the firm said in a report, concurring with the 0.2 percent estimate for June.
It added that competition from big UK retailers had helped keep currency-related inflationary pressures in check.
But King downplayed the effect that the recent entry of a few big UK retailers, such as supermarket chain Tesco Plc, had on the Irish market.
"We've always had multiples (retailers) from the UK. That's been a constant feature of the Irish market. It's just that we have one or two more now," he said.
He also predicted little impact on June inflation from the recent rise in mortgage rates.
"It would be very small because it's only a half percent rise. It's not big enough to feature in our view of the overall number," he said.
Consumer price index data was expected to be released at 1100 GMT on Thursday.
